name: Instructional Designer
description: ⚠⚠⚠ One job title, two federal occupations pulling in opposite directions. Instructional coordinator: $77,440, 60% master's, growing 1–2%. Training and development specialist: $69,280, 78% bachelor's, twice the jobs, twice the openings, growing much faster than average. ⚠⚠ And you cannot major in it — Florida's public institutions awarded 978 credentials in this field and SIX were bachelor's degrees.
credentialNote: ⚠⚠ THERE IS NO LICENCE, NO REQUIRED MAJOR AND NO GATEKEEPER — WHICH MAKES THE PORTFOLIO THE CREDENTIAL. Nothing in this field is licensed by Florida or by any state. What exists is voluntary: ATD's Talent Development Capability Model and its CPTD certification, which requires at least five years of talent development experience and 60 hours of professional development in the last five years — so it is a mid-career credential, not an entry one. ⚠⚠⚠ THE BEST ENTRANT DATA AVAILABLE SAYS THE DEGREE MATTERS AND THE SUBJECT LARGELY DOES NOT. A 2019 survey of instructional designers in higher education (Magruder, Arnold, Moore and Edwards, Online Learning Journal, 104 qualified respondents, ±9%) found 88% held a GRADUATE degree — but only 49% of those degrees were in instructional design or educational technology. ⚠ More than half of working instructional designers in higher education hold a graduate degree in something else. ⚠ Treat that carefully: it is a small survey, from 2017 data, of UPCEA member institutions, and it covers higher education only. It is still the most direct evidence there is, and it points the same way employers do. ⚠⚠ In the CORPORATE sector the requirement inverts — 78% of employers report a bachelor's as the entry requirement for training and development specialists, and what they screen on is a portfolio of work you have actually built.
bodyHtml:
⚠⚠⚠ The same job in two different occupations

RoleSOC2025 medianEmployedOpenings/yrGrowth 2024–34Entry
Instructional coordinator — schools, districts, universities25-9031✅ $77,440232,60021,900⚠⚠ slower than average (1–2%)⚠ 60% master's
Training and development specialist — corporate13-1151$69,280✅ 452,300✅ 43,900✅ much faster (7%+)✅ 78% bachelor's
Training and development manager11-3131✅ $133,00046,4003,800faster (5–6%)71% bachelor's

⚠⚠⚠ “Instructional designer” is a job title that sits across two federal occupations, and they point in opposite directions. The education-sector one pays $8,160 more and is barely growing; the corporate one is nearly twice the size, has twice the annual openings, grows much faster, and does not expect a master's.

⚠⚠ And the ceilings differ more than the entry points. The corporate ladder reaches $133,000 as a training and development manager — on a bachelor's for 71% of them. The education route's higher entry wage is not a higher ceiling.

⚠ So the first decision is not the degree. It is the sector, and it determines whether the master's is worth buying at all.

⚠⚠⚠ You cannot major in this — six bachelor's degrees in the whole state

CodeFL public institutionsCredentialsBachelor's
Curriculum and Instruction (13.0301)10762⚠⚠ 0
Educational/Instructional Technology (13.0501)6216⚠⚠ 6

⚠⚠⚠ 978 credentials, six bachelor's. 642 are master's, 148 research or professional doctorates, and 94 are postbaccalaureate or post-master's certificates. This is a field you enter after a first degree in something else, and that is the normal route rather than a compromise.

⚠⚠ Notice the 94 certificates. They are the cheap route for someone already holding a degree and working — a teacher, a trainer, a subject expert — and they are worth pricing against the master's before assuming the master's is necessary.

⚠⚠ What the entrant data actually says

This is a choice path, so the question is which undergraduate subject helps. The most direct evidence is a 2019 survey of instructional designers working in higher education (Magruder, Arnold, Moore and Edwards, Online Learning Journal; 104 qualified respondents, margin of error ±9%):

Finding
Held a graduate degree✅ 88%
⚠ Whose degree was in instructional design or educational technology⚠⚠ 49%
Experience from a higher education background97%
Working at public higher education institutions61%

⚠⚠⚠ The degree matters; the subject largely does not. More than half of working instructional designers in higher education hold a graduate degree in something else.

⚠ Read the limits with the finding. 104 respondents, ±9%, 2017 data, UPCEA member institutions, higher education only. It is a small survey and it is the best direct evidence that exists — there is no LSAC or AAMC equivalent for this field, and a page that pretended otherwise would be inventing precision.

⚠⚠ What replaces the credential: a portfolio

Nothing here is licensed. The professional body's own credential, ATD's CPTD, requires at least five years of talent development experience and 60 hours of professional development in the last five — a mid-career mark, not a way in.

⚠⚠⚠ So what an employer screens on is work you have actually built. That is unusual among the careers on this site and it has a practical consequence: the cheapest thing you can do for your employability is design something real — a course, a module, a job aid — and be able to explain the analysis behind it.

⚠ It also means the field is genuinely open to career changers in a way licensed professions are not. A teacher, a nurse educator, a technical writer or a subject expert with a portfolio competes with a master's graduate who has none.

⚠ The undergraduate exposure is one course, at 33 institutions

EME2040 Introduction to Technology for Educators is carried by 33 Florida public institutions — more than any other course in the prefix, and taken by most Florida teaching students. The actual instructional design curriculum is graduate: 146 graduate EME course numbers against 132 undergraduate, and the design courses themselves — EME6405 Educational Web Design, EME6209 Digital Video, EME6346 Needs Analysis and Assessment — sit at 6000 level at three to five institutions each.

⚠ The one undergraduate exception worth taking is EME4673 Foundations of Instructional Design, at four institutions (St Petersburg College, UF, UNF, UWF). If your institution carries it, take it — it is the only undergraduate course in Florida that teaches the thing itself.

Necessary skills

  • Needs analysis. The discipline is mostly working out whether training is the answer at all, and it is what separates a designer from a course producer.
  • Learning theory you can apply — the part that survives when the authoring tool changes.
  • Writing. Most instructional design output is words, and clear sequencing is the job.
  • Working with subject experts who know the content and not how to teach it. The 2019 survey found 56% describe the role as a mix of faculty and content development, and the relationship is the hard part.
  • Production skills — authoring tools, video, accessibility, basic web — because somebody has to build it.
  • Evaluation: proving the thing worked, which is what gets budgets renewed.

Advice

⚠⚠⚠ Decide the sector before the degree. Education wants a master's and is growing at 1–2%; corporate wants a bachelor's and a portfolio, has twice the openings, and tops out at $133,000. Buying a master's for a corporate job is optional; buying one for a university job mostly is not.

⚠⚠ Build a portfolio before you buy a credential. Design something real, document the analysis, and show it. In a field with no licence and no required major, this is the whole market signal.

⚠ Price the certificate against the master's. Florida awarded 94 postbaccalaureate and post-master's certificates in this field last year, and if you already hold a degree and a job, that is the efficient route.

⚠ Major in something you can teach from. The survey says more than half of working designers hold a graduate degree outside the field, so subject expertise plus design skill is a normal and competitive combination — and a common route in is being the person in a department who was already good at explaining things.

And if you are a teacher, you are already most of the way there. 33 Florida institutions teach EME2040, the programmes sit in colleges of education, and district instructional coaching is the standard first move.

programs.note: The field — 10 Florida public institutions across the two codes, 978 credentials a year, of which 642 are master's and ⚠⚠ just six are bachelor's. ⚠ Note the 94 postbaccalaureate and post-master's certificates: the short route for someone already holding a degree and working.

⚠⚠ The commonest feeder. These programmes sit in colleges of education, EME2040 Introduction to Technology for Educators is carried by 33 Florida public institutions, and district instructional coaching is the standard first move out of the classroom.

⚠⚠⚠ Named because the LARGER and faster-growing employer is corporate. Training and development specialists number 452,300 against instructional coordinators' 232,600, with 43,900 annual openings and 78% of employers reporting a bachelor's rather than a master's. ⚠ The managerial ceiling there is $133,000.

⚠ The production half — authoring, web delivery, video, accessibility and learning analytics. Florida's graduate curriculum reflects it (EME6405 Educational Web Design, EME6209 Digital Video, EME6208 Interactive Media), and a technical background is a real advantage in a field that screens on built work.

⚠ The discipline the field grew out of — applied learning psychology — and the part that distinguishes a designer from a content producer. ⚠⚠ Named also on availability: psychology is taught at 33 Florida public institutions against this field's 10, and the survey evidence says a graduate degree outside the field is the majority case.

courses.reason: ⚠⚠ Introduction to Technology for Educators — 33 Florida public institutions, more than any other course in the prefix and one of the most widely carried education courses in the state. The undergraduate entry point, and nearly every Florida teaching student takes it.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ It is an introduction to technology FOR TEACHING, not to instructional design. The design curriculum is graduate.

courses.reason: ⚠⚠⚠ Foundations of Instructional Design — only 4 institutions (St Petersburg College, UF, UNF, UWF), and the ONLY undergraduate course in Florida that teaches the discipline itself. If your institution carries it, take it.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ With four carriers this is the hardest useful course in the field to reach as an undergraduate. Check early whether yours has it.

courses.reason: Needs Analysis, Assessment and Data Visualization — 3 institutions (UCF, UNF, USF). ⚠ Needs analysis is the core professional skill: deciding whether training is the answer at all.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ GRADUATE. The EME prefix runs 146 graduate course numbers against 132 undergraduate, and the design courses are all on the graduate side.

courses.reason: Educational Web Design — 4 institutions (FGCU, FIU, UCF, UNF). The production half of the job, and the part a portfolio is built from.
Digital Video — 5 institutions (FAU, FGCU, UCF, UF, USF), the most widely carried graduate EME course. Video is most of modern learning content.
Interactive Media — 3 institutions (FAU, UF, USF). Authoring and interaction design, which is what most corporate e-learning actually is.
Trends and Issues in Technology, Education and Training — 3 institutions (UCF, UNF, USF). The survey course, and the one that covers the corporate side as well as the educational one.
Virtual Teaching and the Digital Educator — 4 institutions (FAU, UCF, UF, UWF). Online course design, which is where higher-education instructional designers spend most of their time.
Introduction to the Teaching Profession — the education foundations entry course, and the usual first step for the teacher route that supplies most people in this field.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Florida numbers introductory education courses several ways (EDF2005, EDF1005, EDG2701). Check your catalogue.

courses.reason: Introduction to Psychology — 33 institutions. Learning theory is the discipline underneath the job, and this is where it starts.
Human Growth and Development — 29 institutions. How people at different ages actually learn, which is the difference between a designer and a content producer.
⚠ English Composition I — 39 institutions. Most instructional design output is words, and clear sequencing is the job. Named deliberately rather than as a general-education box.
English Composition II — 37 institutions. The research and argument half, which is what needs analysis and evaluation reporting actually are.
Elementary Statistics — 39 institutions. Evaluation is what gets a learning budget renewed, and it is statistical work.

Introduction to Programming — named for the production side. ⚠ Not required anywhere, but in a field that screens on built work, being able to handle authoring tools, HTML and basic scripting is a visible advantage.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Florida numbers introductory programming several ways (COP1000, COP2000, CGS1540). Any of them serves the purpose here.

Tasks include developing instructional material and incorporating technology, observing and evaluating teaching staff, planning teacher training, and advising on curriculum development.
